Wing cellules stacked from overlapping plates with the leading edge capped in curved tiles and a deliberate unbroken row of exposed round studs left bare along each upper surface so the aerofoil reads unmistakably as plastic.

Interplane struts assembled from Technic bars threaded through pin-jointed liftarms into a braced N-cage between the upper and lower wing panels, every connection point left visibly proud rather than faired smooth.

Rigging triangulated across the cellule using taut black bar-and-clip runs from spar to spar, each wire a genuine clipped part held under tension so the whole bracing cage reads as individual plastic lengths.

A rotary engine ringed from round 2x2 bricks with short cylinder-brick stubs radiating outward at even intervals, the whole assembly capped by a moulded three-blade propeller element pressed onto a central jumper-plate hub.

The fuselage skinned entirely in smooth tiles laid flush over stacked plates with every panel seam left visible between tile edges, so the underlying brick-built frame reads beneath the covering like structural members showing through fabric.

The cowling nose-ring built from headlight bricks arranged radially on a jumper-plate centre, each headlight socket repurposed as an exhaust stub hole so the ring of moulded cavities reads as a row of open pipe ends.

The grass landing strip laid as a green plate mosaic with individual tuft plant elements pressed at irregular intervals across its surface and a paler row of light-green tiles running the centreline as a mown strip.

The hangar arch stacked course by course from curved slope bricks, the whole shell visibly composed of plastic courses, with hinged panel doors hung on clip plates at the opening so the swing joint is entirely unconcealed.

Undercarriage legs built from Technic-pin uprights with a stretched rubber band lashed horizontally across both legs just above the axle, the band's visible sag and tension reading as a primitive bungee-cord spring unit.

The open cockpit fitted with a small curved windscreen element seated on a single jumper plate ahead of the minifigure, the stud offset centralising the clear part so it sits proud and recognisably plastic above the fuselage line.

The tail-skid formed from a bar clipped beneath a wedge-plate tail section, the clip joint fully exposed at the underside so the single thin bar trails behind the aircraft as an unambiguously parted connection.

Propeller wash represented by a thin trans-clear disc-plate set concentrically on the propeller hub, its transparency and circular seam making the spinning plane read as a brick-built optical device rather than blurred motion.

Exhaust smoke built from white cloud-slope bricks stepping progressively backward from the cylinder-stub ring, each successive slope brick slightly offset so the plume reads as individual stacked plastic pieces rather than a continuous volume.

The hangar rear wall constructed with tan tiles SNOTed vertically onto SNOT brackets, Technic liftarms pinned horizontally behind the tile facing as visible internal bracing, the whole assembly announcing its brick construction at every course.

A wind cone formed from a fabric cloth element threaded lengthwise onto a bar mast planted in a round-brick base, the soft element's visible folds and bar tip left entirely exposed as a deliberate textile-plus-plastic contrast.

Wing trestles supporting the spar built from stacked round bricks on plate bases with Technic liftarms pinned diagonally as cross-bracing, every pin and liftarm hole visible so the support reads as an open-frame scaffold.
Cowling panels hinged open on clip plates to expose the inner ring of cylinder bricks, the hinge plate left flat and unclad so the rotation axis reads as a real part rather than a moulded detail.

An inspection hatch represented by a single smooth tile clipped onto a headlight-brick recess in the fuselage, the tile sitting fractionally proud of the surrounding plate surface so its removability is announced by a visible plastic lip.
The tail plane formed from one large wedge plate with a painted red diagonal band across its plain unmarked upper face and absolutely no printing anywhere on its smooth surface.

The concrete apron laid from light-bley tiles with deliberate single-stud-wide lines of exposed plate studs running across at regular intervals, the stud rows reading as expansion joints in the otherwise smooth pavement.

Float hulls built from wedge plates stacked in a stepping taper toward a boat-shaped keel, each plate edge left exposed at the hull sides so the layered construction reads as a stack of flat plastic sheets rather than a formed hull.

Wing-tip skids formed from bars pressed into clips mounted at each lower-wing end, the bar protruding at a downward angle with the clip joint entirely visible, reading as a deliberate pinned-metal skid in plastic miniature.

The elevator control surface mounted on an actual hinge plate at the tail plane junction, the hinge left open and visibly deflected so the angle between fixed and moving surfaces is an undisguised mechanical joint.

Spatted wheel fairings assembled from curved slope bricks arranged around each moulded tyre on its plate hub, the slope edges meeting without a closing tile so the gaps between bricks hug the rubber and remain openly visible.

A hand-cranked winch drum built from a Technic axle threaded through a stack of round 2x2 bricks with string wound directly onto the brick barrel, the axle ends protruding past the side bricks as unconcealed handle stubs.
